extracted.intended_audience: state air pollution control agencies preparing CAA section 111(d) state plans; owners/operators of affected EGUs; state regulators and plan reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for establishing, applying, and demonstrating compliance with presumptively approvable standards of performance for existing steam-generating EGUs under CAA section 111(d), including BSER determinations, compliance dates, extension mechanisms, and RULOF use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance period and demonstration deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance is required to be demonstrated on an annual (i.e., calendar year) basis. For a unit with a compliance date of January 1, YYYY, the first compliance period is January 1 through December 31 of that year, and the compliance demonstration must occur by March 1 of the following year (e.g., for 2030 compliance period, by March 1, 2031).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States must require affected EGUs to monitor and report for the entire calendar-year compliance period beginning on the compliance date; the end-of-year demonstration deadline is March 1 following the compliance period. This framing clarifies that compliance demonstrations occur after the calendar-year completes, not at the instant the compliance date begins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards must be rate-based or mass-based; mass translation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards of performance must be established as either a rate or, for affected EGUs in certain subcategories, a mass of emissions. If a state chooses to allow mass-based compliance for certain affected EGUs it must first calculate the rate-based emission limitation that corresponds to the presumptive standard of performance, and then explain how it translated that rate-based emission limitation into the mass that constitutes an affected EGU's standard of performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When states incorporate mass-based compliance flexibilities they must document the conversion from the presumptive rate-based limitation to the mass-based standard and provide the rationale/metrics used; see section X.D for further discussion on demonstrating compliance where states incorporate compliance flexibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-term coal-fired BSER and degree of emission limitation (CCS 90% / 88.4% reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For long-term coal-fired steam generating units (those not meeting medium-term specifications), the BSER is CCS with 90 percent capture and the degree of emission limitation is 90 percent capture of the mass of CO2 in the flue gas and an 88.4 percent reduction in emission rate on a lb CO2/MWh-gross basis over an annual calendar-year basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing a standard consists of (1) establishing a source-specific baseline emission performance level and (2) applying the degree of emission limitation. Implementation of CCS at 90% capture translates to an 88.4% reduction in CO2 emission rate; the presumptively approvable standard = baseline * 0.116 (example: baseline 2,000 lb CO2/MWh -> standard 232 lb CO2/MWh). Affected EGUs in this subcategory must also comply with federally enforceable increments of progress (section X.C.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-term coal-fired BSER and degree of emission limitation (40% NG co-firing -> 16% reduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: For medium-term coal-fired steam generating units (those that commit to permanently cease operations before January 1, 2039), the BSER is 40 percent natural gas co-firing on a heat-input basis, which translates to a 16 percent reduction in emission rate on a lb CO2/MWh-gross basis compared to the baseline level of emission performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish baseline emission performance and apply the degree of emission limitation (standard = baseline * 0.84; example: baseline 2,000 lb CO2/MWh -> standard 1,680 lb CO2/MWh). If preexisting co-firing is reflected in the baseline, states must account for that preexisting co-firing by adjusting the degree of emission limitation (example: baseline includes 10% co-firing so the degree is adjusted to achieve an additional 30% co-firing, resulting in a different percent reduction). The standard for this subcategory is rate-based only. If a state places an EGU in this subcategory, the state plan must include that EGU's enforceable commitment to permanently cease operating before Jan 1, 2039 and must include monitoring, reporting, recordkeeping, milestones, and federally enforceable increments of progress (see X.C.3 and X.C.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptive standards for natural gas- and oil-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: Final presumptive standards: base load natural gas- and oil-fired units — 1,400 lb CO2/MWh-gross (annual calendar-year); intermediate load natural gas- and oil-fired units — 1,600 lb CO2/MWh-gross (annual calendar-year). For low-load units, the EPA finalized uniform fuels as the BSER with degrees of emission limitation defined by 130 lb CO2/MMBtu for low-load natural gas-fired units and 170 lb CO2/MMBtu for low-load oil-fired units, and presumptively approvable standards consistent with those values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA finalized these fixed presumptive standards based on low variability in emissions at intermediate and base load and supporting TSD analysis (e.g., >95% of intermediate units have annual rates <1,600 lb CO2/MWh-gross). The rule treats gas and oil units similarly where appropriate given observed operating characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final compliance dates and monitoring/reporting start
rubrics_metrics.description: Finalized compliance dates: January 1, 2030 for most affected steam generating units (including medium-term coal-fired and natural gas- and oil-fired units) and January 1, 2032 for the long-term coal-fired subcategory. These dates are the dates on which affected EGUs must start monitoring and reporting emissions and other relevant data for purposes of demonstrating compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though monitoring/reporting starts on the compliance date, compliance is demonstrated over the calendar year and shown at the end of that calendar year (with the demonstration submission by March 1 of the following year). The compliance date language is used interchangeably in the preamble (compliance date, final compliance date, initial compliance date) but consistently refers to the start of monitoring/reporting obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance date extension mechanism: eligibility, documentation, limits, and process
rubrics_metrics.description: States may include a mechanism in their plans to extend a compliance date (without a plan revision) for affected EGUs that encounter delays in installation of control technology that make it impossible to commence compliance by the plan-specified date, but only where the delay is entirely beyond the owner/operator's control and the owner/operator cannot remedy the delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key features and requirements: (a) Eligible only for affected EGUs installing add-on controls (not for EGUs complying without additional controls); (b) Owner/operator must demonstrate and document: (1) confirmation that relevant increments of progress up to the point of delay have been met (permits, contracts, etc.), (2) documentation (invoices, correspondence) showing the delay is due to third-party action/inaction and that the owner/operator acted consistently with achieving timely compliance, and (3) plans to address and remedy the delay with updated increment-of-progress dates; (c) All documentation must be submitted to the state agency no later than 6 months prior to the compliance date and the owner/operator must notify the EPA Regional Administrator at time of submission and post the application to the Carbon Pollution Standards for EGUs website; (d) State agency approves/disapproves based on its written determination, must notify EPA Regional Administrator and post the determination to the website, and if approved the owner/operator must update website information within 30 days; (e) Maximum extension is 1 year beyond the compliance date; if anticipated delay exceeds 1 year, states should initiate a state plan revision (and consider RULOF) to provide an updated compliance date subject to EPA approval; (f) Extension mechanism is intended to address implementation delays (supply chain, permitting, construction) not to provide more time to assess compliance strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remaining Useful Life and Other Factors (RULOF) — scope and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: States may consider a designated facility's remaining useful life and other factors to apply a less stringent standard of performance or a longer compliance schedule only where the facility's circumstances are 'fundamentally different' from the circumstances the EPA considered, and those fundamental differences make it unreasonable for the facility to achieve the degree of emission limitation or compliance schedule in the emission guideline. The RULOF provisions in 40 CFR 60.24a (as revised Nov 2023) govern these demonstrations and procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Important constraints and procedures: (a) The relevant question is whether the facility can reasonably achieve the degree of emission limitation in the emission guideline (not merely whether it can implement the BSER); if the facility can achieve the degree of limitation via a different system, RULOF cannot be used to apply a less stringent standard; (b) The state bears the burden to demonstrate under 40 CFR 60.24a(e)-(f) that less-stringent standards or longer schedules are necessary and limited to addressing the fundamental differences; (c) In determining a less-stringent standard, the state must evaluate systems of emission reduction using the factors EPA considered — technical feasibility, amount of emission reductions, cost of achieving reductions, any non-air quality health and environmental impacts, and energy requirements — and may consider other facility-specific factors as justified; (d) If the less-stringent standard is based on an operating condition within the facility's control, the state plan must include that operating condition as an enforceable requirement and include monitoring, reporting, and recordkeeping for implementation and enforcement; (e) States must include documentation of meaningful engagement with pertinent stakeholders and consideration of communities most impacted by or vulnerable to the EGU's impacts when proposing a RULOF-based deviation; (f) States may always adopt more stringent standards or faster compliance schedules without invoking RULOF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumptively approvable standards serve as the default floor
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, the standards of performance that states establish for designated facilities must be no less stringent than the presumptively approvable standards of performance specified in these emission guidelines (40 CFR 60.24a(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A state seeking to apply a less stringent standard or longer compliance schedule must rely on the RULOF process and demonstrate why the presumptively approvable standard is unreasonable for the particular facility; absent such a valid demonstration, state standards must meet or exceed the presumptively approvable standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federally enforceable increments of progress and milestones requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected EGUs in certain subcategories (e.g., long-term and medium-term coal-fired subcategories) must comply with federally enforceable increments of progress and specified milestones to implement required control technologies or commitments (e.g., commitments to cease operations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State plans must include provisions for the implementation and enforcement of these increments of progress and milestones, including monitoring, reporting, and recordkeeping, and the EPA expects these milestones to help ensure timely implementation and identify issues early (see sections X.C.3 and X.C.4 for details).
